slides.title: The Cooling Coffee Cup
slides.alt: The cup of coffee and its thermometer, drawn large

setup.preamble: A cup of coffee is left on a table in a room. It loses heat to the air, quickly at first.
setup.para: Two readings are taken. At the start, $t=0$, the coffee is $92\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Two minutes later, at $t=2$, it is $78.7\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Time $t$ is in minutes.

scene.alt: A cup of coffee on a table and a thermometer beside the graph

slides.title: Where does it settle? (1 of 2)
slides.stem: Predict: after a very long time, what temperature does the coffee approach?

walk.cap: Heat flows from hot to cool
walk.note: The coffee loses heat to the air in the room, quickly at first.

scene.alt: A cup of coffee on a table and a thermometer beside the graph

slides.title: Where does it settle? (2 of 2)
slides.stem: Predict: after a very long time, what temperature does the coffee approach?

walk.note: Once it is as warm as the room there is nothing left to lose, so the temperature stops falling. It does not go to $0\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

scene.alt: A cup of coffee on a table and a thermometer beside the graph

slides.title: Fit the model (1 of 3)
slides.stem: The model is $T=k(0.9)^t+c$, with $t$ in minutes. Use the two readings to find $k$ and $c$.

scene.alt: A cup of coffee on a table and a thermometer beside the graph

slides.title: Fit the model (2 of 3)
slides.stem: The model is $T=k(0.9)^t+c$, with $t$ in minutes. Use the two readings to find $k$ and $c$.

walk.cap: Subtract the second equation from the first

scene.alt: A cup of coffee on a table and a thermometer beside the graph

slides.title: Fit the model (3 of 3)
slides.stem: The model is $T=k(0.9)^t+c$, with $t$ in minutes. Use the two readings to find $k$ and $c$.

walk.note: $c$ is the horizontal asymptote: the temperature of the room, $22\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
Two readings fix the two unknowns $k$ and $c$.

scene.alt: A cup of coffee on a table and a thermometer beside the graph

slides.title: When can it be drunk? (1 of 2)
slides.stem: It can be drunk at $50\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ or below. After how many whole minutes is that first true?

scene.alt: A cup of coffee on a table and a thermometer beside the graph

slides.title: When can it be drunk? (2 of 2)
slides.stem: It can be drunk at $50\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ or below. After how many whole minutes is that first true?

walk.note: After $8$ minutes it is still $52.1\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. After $9$ it is $49.1\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Round up, not to the nearest whole number.

scene.alt: A cup of coffee on a table and a thermometer beside the graph

slides.title: The Typing Student
slides.alt: The laptop and its words-per-minute gauge, drawn large

setup.preamble: A student practises typing, and her speed is timed after each stretch of practice.
setup.para: After $1$ hour of practice she types $20$ words per minute. After $10$ hours she types $43.03$ words per minute. The practice time $h$ is in hours.

facts.html: $h$ is in hours and $S$ in words per minute

scene.alt: A laptop and a words-per-minute gauge beside the graph

slides.title: Speed after 100 hours (1 of 2)
slides.stem: Predict: how fast does she type after $100$ hours?

walk.note: Ten times the practice added $23.03$ words per minute.

scene.alt: A laptop and a words-per-minute gauge beside the graph

slides.title: Speed after 100 hours (2 of 2)
slides.stem: Predict: how fast does she type after $100$ hours?

walk.note: Another tenfold increase adds about the same again. Steady gains would give about $270$, so the gains are slowing.

scene.alt: A laptop and a words-per-minute gauge beside the graph
A laptop and a words-per-minute gauge beside the graph

walk.note: Two readings fix two unknowns, as with the coffee.

scene.alt: A laptop and a words-per-minute gauge beside the graph

slides.title: Where the model breaks (1 of 2)
slides.stem: What does the model give at $0.1$ hours and at $5000$ hours? Name one specific limitation.

walk.note: A negative typing speed is impossible.
Still rising after 5000 hours, with no ceiling.

scene.alt: A laptop and a words-per-minute gauge beside the graph

slides.title: Where the model breaks (2 of 2)
slides.stem: What does the model give at $0.1$ hours and at $5000$ hours? Name one specific limitation.

walk.note: The model gives a negative speed for $h<0.135$, so it fails for very little practice. It also never levels off, so it cannot hold for very long practice. Say which, and say why.

scene.alt: A laptop and a words-per-minute gauge beside the graph

slides.title: Lemon, Tomato and Water
slides.alt: The pH strip with lemon juice, tomato and water, drawn large

setup.preamble: A pH strip tells how acidic a liquid is. A food-science class tests lemon juice, a tomato, and pure water with one.
setup.para: Lemon juice has pH $2.0$ and a tomato has pH $4.4$. Here, $\mathrm{pH}=-\log_{10}[\mathrm{H}^+]$, where $[\mathrm{H}^+]$ is the concentration of hydrogen ions. The graph measures it in mmol/L.

facts.html: $[\mathrm{H}^+]$ is in mmol/L on the graph

scene.alt: A pH strip with lemon juice, tomato and water beside the graph

slides.title: How much stronger? (1 of 2)
slides.stem: Predict: how many times stronger (more $[\mathrm{H}^+]$) is the lemon juice than the tomato?

walk.cap: Each pH step is a factor of $10$
walk.note: Lowering the pH by $1$ multiplies $[\mathrm{H}^+]$ by $10$.

scene.alt: A pH strip with lemon juice, tomato and pure water beside the graph

slides.title: How much stronger? (2 of 2)
slides.stem: Predict: how many times stronger (more $[\mathrm{H}^+]$) is the lemon juice than the tomato?

walk.cap: The lemon is $2.4$ steps below the tomato
walk.note: $2.4$ steps lies between $2$ and $3$, so the answer is between $100$ and $1000$: about $250$. Question 3 finds it exactly.

scene.alt: A pH strip with lemon juice, tomato and pure water beside the graph

slides.title: Both directions (1 of 2)
slides.stem: Find the pH when $[\mathrm{H}^+]=0.0003$. Find $[\mathrm{H}^+]$ when the pH is $6.6$. Give the second answer in standard form.

scene.alt: A pH strip with lemon juice, tomato and pure water beside the graph

slides.title: Both directions (2 of 2)
slides.stem: Find the pH when $[\mathrm{H}^+]=0.0003$. Find $[\mathrm{H}^+]$ when the pH is $6.6$. Give the second answer in standard form.

walk.cap: Undo the log with a power of $10$
walk.note: Undoing $\log_{10}$ means raising $10$ to the power.

scene.alt: A pH strip with lemon juice, tomato and pure water beside the graph

slides.title: Exactly how much stronger? (1 of 2)
slides.stem: Find exactly how many times stronger the lemon juice is than the tomato.

scene.alt: A pH strip with lemon juice, tomato and pure water beside the graph

slides.title: Exactly how much stronger? (2 of 2)
slides.stem: Find exactly how many times stronger the lemon juice is than the tomato.

walk.cap: The shortcut: subtract the pH values, then raise $10$ to the difference
walk.note: Compare by subtracting, never by dividing: $4.4\div 2.0=2.2$ is wrong. The lemon is about $251$ times stronger.

scene.alt: A pH strip with lemon juice, tomato and pure water beside the graph

slides.eyebrow: Beyond the story · Exponential and log models around us
slides.title: Where else does it happen?

items.title: Cooling cups
what: How fast hot water cools in different cups
why: Heat leaves faster when the water is much hotter than the room
The temperature levels off at room temperature
exp: Set up
Fill a glass, a mug and a foam cup with hot tap water
Stand a thermometer in each
Every 2 minutes for 30 minutes, read each one
Also read the room temperature
Plot temperature against time

items.title: Light fading in water
what: The brightness of a torch beam after it passes through layers of water
why: Each layer absorbs the same fraction of the light
So brightness falls exponentially with depth
exp: Set up
Add 3 drops of milk to a litre of water
Pour it into identical clear cups
Shine a torch through 1, 2, 3 and 4 cups onto a phone light meter
Record the reading for each
Plot brightness against cups

items.title: Diluting lemon juice
what: The pH of lemon juice diluted again and again
why: Each tenfold dilution should raise the pH by about $1$
The pH is a log scale
exp: Set up
Make juice, then 1 in 10, 1 in 100, 1 in 1000
Use pH strips
Read the pH of each
Plot pH against the dilution as a power of $10$
Compare with the model

items.title: Car depreciation
what: The asking price of one car model against its age
why: A car loses about the same fraction of its value each year
The price falls quickly, then slowly
exp: Find the data
Choose one model on a used-car site
Note price and age for 15 listings
Record age and price in a table
Plot price against age
Fit an exponential and read the yearly loss

items.title: Learning curves
what: The time taken to solve a puzzle on each attempt
why: Later gains shrink, as in the typing scene
exp: Pick a skill, such as a cube or a typing test
Do it 5 times a day for 3 weeks
Record the mean score each day
Plot score against day and fit $a+b\ln x$

items.title: Sound and distance
what: The sound level in decibels at increasing distances from a speaker
why: Decibels are a log scale of sound intensity
Intensity falls with the square of the distance
exp: Set up
Play a steady tone from a phone
Use a decibel app on another phone
Read the level at 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 metres
Plot level against the log of distance
Compare the slope with the model

items.title: Earthquake magnitudes
what: The number of earthquakes of each magnitude in a year, from public data
why: Magnitude is a log scale of energy
So a log graph of the counts is a straight line
exp: Download a year of quakes from a public catalogue
Count how many fall in each magnitude band
Plot the counts on a log scale
Find the factor for each step up

items.title: Pitch and frequency
what: The frequency of each fret on a ukulele string
why: Each fret raises the pitch by the same ratio
So frequency is exponential in the fret number
exp: Read the open string on a tuner app
Read the frequency at each fret up to the 12th
Plot frequency against fret number
Find the ratio per fret and test $2^{1/12}$
